subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Assalaamu alaykum, young scientist! In this unit you are going to explore one of the biggest and most exciting questions in all of science: why do we have day and night? Every single morning the sky grows bright over the Indian Ocean, and every evening it turns dark and the stars come out over the savanna. You have watched this happen your whole life. Now you will finally discover the wonderful secret behind it.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

outcomes: Explain that Earth spins (rotates) on its axis, and that this spinning gives us day and night.
Describe how the Sun appears to move across the sky from east to west, and explain why it only *appears* to move.
Tell the story of a day: sunrise in the east, the high midday sun, and sunset in the west.
Observe and describe how shadows change in length and direction through the day.
Explain that a shadow forms when an object blocks the light of the Sun.
Understand that when it is day where you live, it is night on the other side of Earth.
Explain that the Sun is a star — a huge ball of hot, glowing gas.
Use the Sun and shadows to help you find direction and guess the time.
Stay safe by never looking straight at the Sun.

concepts.title: Earth Is a Giant Spinning Ball
concepts.explanation:
Let us start with something surprising. When you stand still in your yard, it feels like you are not moving at all. The ground feels solid and steady under your feet. But the truth is amazing: you are moving right now, very fast, because the whole Earth is spinning. Earth is a giant ball, and it turns around and around, like a football spinning on the tip of a finger, or like a spinning top that a child sets going.

Earth is so enormous, and it spins so smoothly, that you cannot feel it moving at all. Think of riding in a smooth car or a boat on calm water. If you close your eyes, you can hardly tell you are moving. Earth is like that, but much, much bigger and smoother. It takes Earth one whole day — 24 hours — to spin around one time.

Now here is the important part. The Sun shines its light on Earth from one side, like a very bright lamp. But a ball can only be lit on one side at a time. The side of Earth that faces the Sun is bright — that side is having day. The side that faces away from the Sun is dark — that side is having night. As Earth keeps spinning, your town is carried around from the dark side into the light, and then later back into the dark again.

So when the sun rises in the morning, the Sun is not really climbing up into the sky. Instead, your part of Earth is turning to face the Sun. And when the sun sets in the evening, the Sun is not really going down. Instead, your part of Earth is turning away from the Sun. This is the big secret of day and night. Read it one more time slowly, because it is the most important idea in the whole unit: day and night happen because Earth spins.

It is easy to believe the Sun is the thing that moves, because that is exactly how it looks from where you stand. For a very long time, wise people everywhere believed the Sun travelled around the Earth. But good scientists learned to look more carefully, to test their ideas, and to change their minds when they found the truth. This is a wonderful lesson for you as a young scientist: the way something *looks* is not always the way it really *is*. That is why we do experiments and think hard, instead of just believing the first thing we see. In this unit you will practise looking beyond what your eyes tell you, to understand what is truly happening in the sky above your town.

Did You Know? Earth is spinning so fast that a town near the middle of Earth, like Mogadishu or Nairobi, is carried along at over 1,600 kilometres every hour — faster than an aeroplane! You do not feel it because everything around you is moving smoothly together.
concepts.example: You can prove this idea to yourself with a simple picture in your head. Imagine a torch (a flashlight) shining on an orange in a dark room. Only the front of the orange is lit; the back is in shadow. Now turn the orange slowly. A little mark on the orange moves from the lit side, into the dark side, and back again. That little mark is like your town, and the orange is like Earth. In your Experiments book you will do exactly this with a ball and a torch, and you will see day and night with your own eyes.

concepts.title: Why the Sun Seems to Travel Across the Sky
concepts.explanation:
Go outside in the morning (but remember — never look straight at the Sun!). Notice where the Sun is. In the early morning, the Sun is low in the sky in the east. That is the direction of the sunrise, out over the Indian Ocean if you live on the coast. Later, in the middle of the day, the Sun is high up, almost straight above your head. By the evening, the Sun is low again, but now in the west, and it slowly sinks until it is gone.

It really does look like the Sun is walking across the sky, from east to west, every single day. People long ago believed the Sun truly moved around the Earth. But now we know the real answer, and it is even more wonderful: the Sun stays still, and it is Earth that is turning. Because you are standing on spinning Earth, the Sun only *appears* to move. We call this the Sun's apparent movement — apparent means 'how it looks', not 'what is really happening'.

Here is a way to feel this for yourself. Sit on a chair that can turn around, in the middle of a room. Look at a lamp or a window. Now slowly turn the chair around. What happens? The lamp seems to slide across in front of you and move around the room — but you know the lamp did not move at all. You moved. The Sun in the sky is just like that lamp. It looks like it moves, but really you and all of Earth are turning.

Did You Know? The Sun always rises in the east and sets in the west, everywhere on Earth — in Hargeisa, in Dar es Salaam, in Kampala, and in every country in the world. Travellers and sailors have used this for thousands of years to find their way.
concepts.example: Because the Sun's path is always the same, it helps us in daily life. When you see the sunrise, you know that way is east. When you see the sunset, you know that way is west. If you spread your arms with your right hand toward the sunrise, then in front of you is north and behind you is south. This is how people crossing the wide savanna, or sailing along the coast, could find their direction long before there were maps on a phone. The sky was their map.

concepts.title: The Story of Shadows
concepts.explanation:
A shadow is a dark shape that appears when something blocks the light. Light from the Sun travels in straight lines. When your body, or a tree, or a house stands in the way, the light cannot pass through you, so a dark shape falls on the ground behind you. That dark shape is your shadow. You need three things to make a shadow: a light source (the Sun), an object to block the light (like you), and a surface for the shadow to fall on (like the ground or a wall).

The most exciting thing about shadows is that they change through the day, and they change in a pattern you can predict. Let us follow a shadow from morning to evening. Imagine Amina places a straight stick in the sand in her yard in Garissa and watches its shadow all day.

In the early morning, the Sun is low in the east. When the Sun is low, shadows are very long. Amina's stick makes a long shadow that stretches far across the ground, pointing toward the west, away from the Sun. At midday, the Sun is high overhead. When the Sun is high, shadows are very short. Now the stick's shadow is tiny, just a small dark patch at its feet. In the late afternoon, the Sun is low again in the west, and the shadow grows long again, but now it points toward the east.

Can you see the pattern? Shadows are long in the morning, short at midday, and long again in the evening. And shadows always point away from the Sun. In the morning the Sun is in the east, so shadows point west. In the evening the Sun is in the west, so shadows point east. Once you know this pattern, a shadow can tell you roughly what time of day it is — it is like a clock made of sunlight.

Did You Know? Long ago, people built clever shadow clocks called sundials. A sundial is just a stick that casts a shadow onto marked lines. As the Sun moves across the sky, the shadow moves across the lines and shows the time. You will build your very own sundial in the Experiments book!
concepts.example: This shadow pattern is helpful in real life in a hot, sunny land. When the midday sun is strong and the shadows are short, there is very little shade, and it is the hottest part of the day. That is a good time to rest indoors or under a big acacia tree, and to drink plenty of clean water. In the morning and evening, when shadows are long, the air is cooler and it is a better time to play outside, herd the goats, or work in the garden. Understanding shadows helps you plan your day wisely.

concepts.title: The Sun Is a Star
concepts.explanation:
When you look up on a clear night, far from the town lights, you can see thousands of tiny points of light. Those are stars. A star is a huge ball of hot, glowing gas that makes its own light. The stars look tiny to us only because they are unbelievably far away.

Here is a surprise: our Sun is a star too! The Sun does not look like the tiny stars of the night. It looks big and bright and warm. Why? Because the Sun is the closest star to Earth. All the other stars are so far away that they shrink to little dots, but the Sun is our neighbour, so we can feel its heat and see its bright light filling the whole sky.

The Sun is far bigger than Earth — so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. And it is very, very far away, so far that even the fastest aeroplane could never reach it. Yet its light and warmth cross all that space to reach us. Every plant that grows — the mango trees, the maize, the grass the cattle eat — uses the Sun's light to make its food. Without the Sun there would be no light, no warmth, no plants, and no life. The Sun is the most important thing in our sky.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The Sun's light takes about eight minutes to travel all the way to Earth. So when you feel the warm morning sun on your face, that sunlight actually left the Sun eight minutes before it touched you!

concepts.title: Day and Night Around the World
concepts.explanation:
Because Earth is a ball, and the Sun can only light one side at a time, something interesting is always true: when it is day where you live, it is night on the far side of Earth. Right now, while children in Mogadishu are eating breakfast in the morning sun, children on the opposite side of the world are fast asleep in the dark of night.

This is why different places have different times. As Earth spins, the morning sun reaches some countries first and other countries later. The sun rises over the coast of Kenya and Somalia before it rises over lands far to the west. Everyone gets their turn in the sunlight as Earth turns them toward the Sun. We call these different time areas time zones.
concepts.example: You can understand this with your ball and torch. Put a small sticker on the ball to be your town, and another sticker on the opposite side to be a faraway country. Shine the torch. When your town's sticker is in the light (day), the far sticker is in the dark (night). Turn the ball, and they swap. This simple model shows you exactly why the whole world cannot have daytime all at once.

concepts.title: Hot Days, Cool Nights, and the Seasons
concepts.explanation:
You have surely noticed that the middle of the day is hot, but the night can feel surprisingly cool, especially in the dry, semi-arid land away from the coast. Why? During the day, the Sun pours its warmth onto the ground and heats it up. At night, your part of Earth is turned away from the Sun, so no new warmth arrives, and the heat slowly escapes into the sky. That is why nights in the desert can feel cold even after a very hot day. A wise family keeps a blanket ready even in a hot land.

Over a whole year, the weather also changes in a pattern we call the seasons. In East Africa we do not have deep snow and ice like some cold countries. Instead we have times of rain and times of dryness — the long rains, the short rains, and the dry season. These seasons come because Earth travels all the way around the Sun once each year, and this long journey slowly changes the weather and the length of the daylight. Farmers watch the seasons closely to know when to plant their crops, and herders move their animals to find fresh grass and water. You will learn much more about seasons and Earth's yearly journey when you are a little older.

Near the middle of Earth, close to the imaginary line called the equator, the Sun climbs very high and its light is strong and direct. This is why the sun in East Africa feels so powerful, and why it is so important to wear a hat, stay in the shade during the hottest hours, and drink plenty of clean, safe water. The same strong sun that can tire you out is also a gift: it can be used to dry clothes and food quickly, and special solar panels can catch its energy to make electricity, even in a village far from any power line.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Muslims all over the world use the Moon and the Sun to keep time for worship. The five daily prayers follow the Sun's position — Fajr near sunrise, Dhuhr after midday, and Maghrib right at sunset. And the month of Ramadan is found by watching for the thin crescent Moon. Watching the sky has always helped people order their days.

explorations.title: Day and Night with a Ball and a Torch
explorations.context: To model how Earth's spinning makes day and night, using a ball as Earth and a torch as the Sun. Make a Guess (Hypothesis) Before you begin, guess: If I shine a torch on one side of a ball, what will the other side be like? Will the whole ball be lit, or only part of it? Say your guess out loud or write it down. What You Need (all from home) A ball, an orange, or a round fruit (this is your Earth). A torch or the light on a phone (this is your Sun). A small sticker, or a tiny piece of paper and tape (this is your town). A darkened room (close the curtains, or do it at night). What To Do Stick your sticker onto the ball. This spot is your town on Earth. Make the room dark. Ask an adult for help if you need it. Hold the torch still and shine it on one side of the ball. This is the Sun's light. Look at the ball. Which part is bright (day)? Which part is dark (night)? Turn the ball slowly so your sticker moves from the bright side toward the dark side. Watch your town go from day into night. Keep turning until your sticker comes back into the light. Your town has had a whole day and night! Write Down What You See (Recording Sheet) Question Bright or Dark? Is that Day or Night? When my town faced the torch When my town faced away from the torch What the opposite side of the ball was like when my town had day Think About It (Analysis) Was the whole ball ever lit up at once? Why not? When your town had day, what did the opposite side of the ball have? What made your town change from day to night — did the torch move, or did the ball turn?

explorations.title: The Shadow Stick Through the Day
explorations.context: To watch how a shadow changes length and direction from morning to evening, and to discover the shadow pattern for yourself. Make a Guess (Hypothesis) Guess: Will my shadow stick's shadow be longer in the morning or at midday? Which way do you think the shadow will point in the morning? What You Need: A straight stick, a pencil pushed into a lump of clay, or a bottle stood upright. A sunny outdoor spot where the ground does not change all day (sand or dirt is perfect). Small stones, chalk, or bottle caps to mark the shadow. A ruler or a piece of string to measure length (optional). What To Do: Early in the morning, push your stick firmly into the ground in a sunny spot so it stands straight up. Find the shadow it makes on the ground. Place a stone at the tip (the far end) of the shadow. Measure how long the shadow is, from the stick to the stone. Write it down with the time. Come back at midday (around noon). Mark the new shadow tip with another stone and measure again. Come back in the late afternoon. Mark and measure the shadow one more time. Remember the safety rule: look only at the shadow on the ground, NEVER at the Sun.

explorations.title: Build Your Own Sundial (Shadow Clock)
explorations.context: To build a simple shadow clock, like the ones people used long before modern clocks, and use it to tell the time from the Sun. Make a Guess (Hypothesis) Guess: Can a stick and its shadow really help me tell the time? How do you think it might work? What You Need: A paper plate, a flat piece of cardboard, or a smooth patch of sand. A straight stick or a pencil. A pen, chalk, or small stones to make marks. A real clock or a phone, just for this one day, to label the hours. What To Do: Push the stick straight up through the middle of your plate or into the sand, in a sunny place that stays sunny all day. Every hour, on the hour, look where the shadow falls. Draw a line along the shadow and write the time next to it (for example, 8, 9, 10). Keep doing this through the day. Each hour the shadow will be in a slightly different place. The next sunny day, do not use the clock. Just look at where the shadow falls and read the time from your marks!

explorations.title: The Spinning Chair and the Moving Sun
explorations.context: To feel with your own body why the Sun seems to move, even though it is really you (and Earth) who are turning. Make a Guess (Hypothesis) Guess: If I spin slowly while looking at a lamp, will the lamp seem to move, even though it stays still? What You Need A chair that can turn, or just a clear space where you can turn your body around slowly. A lamp, a bright window, or a candle placed safely across the room (this is the Sun). What To Do Sit or stand in the middle of the room. Look at the lamp — that is your 'Sun'. Very slowly, turn yourself around in a full circle. Keep your eyes looking ahead, not glued to the lamp. Notice how the lamp seems to slide across your view and travel around the room. Stop and think: did the lamp actually move? Or did you move?

workedExamples.title: Reading Shadows and the Sun
workedExamples.prompt: Sometimes in science we measure things and work out an answer step by step. Let us do two examples together. Read each step slowly and make sure you understand it before moving on.
workedExamples.solution:
Worked Example 1: How long is the shadow?

Hassan puts a stick in the ground in the morning and measures its shadow with a ruler. Then he measures it again at midday and again in the late afternoon. Here is what he found:

Time of Day

Where the Sun Is

workedExamples.solution:

Where the Sun Is

Shadow Length

workedExamples.title: 2: Using shadows to guess the time
workedExamples.prompt: Khadija is playing outside with no clock nearby. She looks at the shadow of the tall water tank. The shadow is very short, almost hiding under the tank, and the ground is very hot. What time of day is it, and in which direction should she look to find shade soon?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1: A very short shadow means the Sun is high in the sky. Step 2: The Sun is highest at midday, around noon. So it is about the middle of the day. Step 3: After midday the Sun moves toward the west, so shadows will start to grow and point toward the east. Khadija can expect longer, cooler shadows on the east side of buildings as the afternoon goes on. She decides to rest in the shade and drink some water until the strong midday heat passes. Clever thinking, Khadija!

Reading Time: Yusuf and the Sunrise

Read this short story, then answer the questions with your tutor or family.

Yusuf lived in a small town near the coast, close to the wide blue Indian Ocean. He loved to wake early for the Fajr prayer, before the sky was light. One morning, after prayers, his grandmother took his hand and led him to the doorway. 'Watch the east, Yusuf,' she said softly. At first the sky was grey and quiet. Then a thin line of pink and gold appeared far away over the water. Slowly the light grew brighter, and the golden edge of the Sun peeked over the sea. The whole world turned warm and bright. The roosters crowed, the fishermen called to each other, and a long shadow stretched out behind Yusuf across the sand, pointing away from the rising Sun. 'Why does the Sun come every morning, Grandmother?' Yusuf asked. She smiled. 'It is not the Sun that comes to us, my child. It is our great Earth that turns to face the Sun, the way you turn your face toward someone who is speaking to you. Every morning the Earth turns our town toward the light, and every evening it turns us away again to rest.' Yusuf looked at his long shadow and thought about the enormous Earth carrying him gently toward the morning. He felt very small, and very thankful.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: What causes day and night? (a) The Sun turns off at night (b) Earth spins (c) Clouds cover the Sun (d) The Moon blocks the Sun
workedExamples.solution: (b) Earth spins. Day and night are caused by Earth turning, not by the Sun switching off.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: How long does Earth take to spin around one time? (a) One hour (b) One week (c) One day (24 hours) (d) One year
workedExamples.solution: (c) One day (24 hours). Earth makes one full spin every 24 hours.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: In which direction does the Sun rise? (a) North (b) South (c) East (d) West

rules.title: Why We Have Day and Night
rules.text: The three most important ideas: 1) Earth spins once a day, and that gives us day and night. 2) The Sun only seems to move because we are moving. 3) Never, ever look straight at the Sun — use shadows to know where it is.

terms: The round planet we live on; it spins once a day and orbits the Sun once a year.

A time of year with its own weather (rainy or dry).

vocabulary.meaning: The round planet we live on; it spins once a day and orbits the Sun once a year.
vocabulary.example: In this unit you will learn that this pattern is caused by our giant planet Earth spinning like a top.

vocabulary.meaning: The star at the centre of our solar system that gives us light and heat.
vocabulary.example: When the sun rises over Mombasa or Kismaayo, the fishermen push their boats onto the water, the roosters crow, and your family wakes for the Fajr prayer.

vocabulary.meaning: To turn around and around like a top.
The invisible line Earth spins around.
vocabulary.example: Explain that Earth spins (rotates) on its axis, and that this spinning gives us day and night.

vocabulary.meaning: Time when your part of Earth faces the Sun (light).
vocabulary.example: By the middle of the day the sun is high and strong, the ground is hot under your feet, and the shadows grow small.

vocabulary.meaning: Time when your part of Earth faces away from the Sun (dark).
vocabulary.example: Explain that Earth spins (rotates) on its axis, and that this spinning gives us day and night.

vocabulary.meaning: When the Sun appears in the east.
vocabulary.example: Sunrise over the Indian Ocean is beautiful and pink.

vocabulary.meaning: When the Sun sinks in the west.
vocabulary.example: After sunset the air in the desert cools quickly.

vocabulary.meaning: A dark shape made when an object blocks light.
vocabulary.example: Explain that a shadow forms when an object blocks the light of the Sun.

vocabulary.meaning: A huge ball of hot glowing gas that makes its own light.
vocabulary.example: You will find out that the sun is really a star — the closest star to us — and that it gives our world the light and warmth that every plant, animal, and person needs to live.

vocabulary.meaning: A time of year with its own weather (rainy or dry).
vocabulary.example: A time of year with its own weather, like the dry season or the rainy season.

It looks that way from the ground.
Thinking the Sun turns off at night.
We cannot see it, so it seems gone.
Thinking it is night everywhere at once.
It is night where we are.
Thinking the Sun is not a star.
It looks bigger and brighter than night stars.
A shadow looks solid and still.

connections.text: You already learned that light travels in straight lines and shadows form when light is blocked. This unit uses that to explain shadows made by the Sun.
Moon and Planets (future units): The words *orbit*, *star*, and *planet* will help you when you explore the Moon, the planets, and the whole solar system.
Directions (east, west, north, south) and time zones connect science to maps and the wider world.
The Sun's position marks the times of the daily prayers, and the crescent Moon marks the start of months like Ramadan.
Measuring shadow lengths and comparing them (longer, shorter) uses your measuring and comparing skills.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: In your own words, explain why we have day and night.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: We have day and night because Earth spins. When your part of Earth faces the Sun it is day; when it faces away it is night.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Is the Sun really moving across the sky? Explain what is really happening.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: No, the Sun is not really moving across the sky. Earth is spinning, which makes the Sun appear to move.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe how a shadow changes from the morning to the middle of the day.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: In the morning the shadow is long (the Sun is low). By midday the shadow becomes short (the Sun is high overhead).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What three things do you need to make a shadow?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: You need a light source (the Sun), an object to block the light, and a surface for the shadow to fall on.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is it night on the other side of the world when it is day where you live?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because Earth is a ball, the Sun can only light half of it at once. The half turned toward the Sun has day; the half turned away has night.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why do we say the Sun is a star?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The Sun is a star because it is a huge ball of hot, glowing gas that makes its own light. It looks bigger and brighter only because it is the closest star to us.

rounds.explanation: One day (24 hours). Earth makes one full spin every 24 hours.

rounds.prompt: When is the Sun highest in the sky?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Midday. The Sun is highest around noon, in the middle of the day.

games.title: Real-Life Round: Shadow
games.description: Practise shadow through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: When it is daytime where you live, the opposite side of Earth has:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Night. Only half of Earth faces the Sun at once, so the far side is dark.

rounds.prompt: What should you NEVER do when studying the Sun?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Look straight at the Sun. This can badly hurt your eyes — always use shadows instead.

rounds.prompt: In which direction does the Sun rise?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: East. The Sun always appears to rise in the east.

rounds.prompt: When the Sun is high in the sky, shadows are:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Very short. A high Sun makes short shadows; a low Sun makes long shadows.

games.title: Spot the Error: Star
games.description: Practise star through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: To make a shadow you need a light source, a surface, and:
choices: An object to block the light
rounds.answer: An object to block the light
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: An object to block the light. Light, an object, and a surface are the three things needed.

rounds.prompt: What causes day and night?
choices: The Sun turns off at night
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Earth spins. Day and night are caused by Earth turning, not by the Sun switching off.

rounds.prompt: In which direction does the Sun set?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: West. The Sun always appears to set in the west.

rounds.prompt: Which way does a shadow point?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Away from the Sun. Light is blocked by the object, so the shadow falls on the far side.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Season

rounds.prompt: Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky?
choices: It is pulled by the Moon
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Earth is spinning. The Sun only appears to move because we are turning with Earth.

rounds.prompt: How long does Earth take to spin around one time?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: One day (24 hours). Earth makes one full spin every 24 hours.

rounds.prompt: When is the Sun highest in the sky?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Midday. The Sun is highest around noon, in the middle of the day.

rounds.prompt: The Sun is really a:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Star. The Sun is a star — the closest one to Earth.

selfAssessment: I can explain that Earth spins (rotates) on its axis, and that this spinning gives us day and night.
I can describe how the Sun appears to move across the sky from east to west, and explain why it only *appears* to move.
I can tell the story of a day: sunrise in the east, the high midday sun, and sunset in the west.
I can observe and describe how shadows change in length and direction through the day.
I can explain that a shadow forms when an object blocks the light of the Sun.
I can understand that when it is day where you live, it is night on the other side of Earth.
I can explain that the Sun is a star — a huge ball of hot, glowing gas.
I can use the Sun and shadows to help you find direction and guess the time.
